_doc: Guide v2 content for /guides/concept-to-texture-set/. Every step is written from the linked official docs (checked 2026-10-17). Videos must be from the vendor's/project's own YouTube channel (verified via oEmbed) and show a current version. Images only with a clear reuse licence, stored in src/assets/guides/<slug>/.
result: A tileable AI-generated colour texture plus height, normal, roughness and AO maps, checked in Blender and set up as a material in Unreal, Unity or Godot.

shared.h: Generate a flat, tileable source texture
do: In Scenario, open Scenario Texture (the Textures flow).
Describe only the material, like "wet sand, ripple marks", with no scene or perspective.
Set the size (default 1024 x 1024, in multiples of 16) and turn on Erase Seam.
If seams remain, raise Overlap for big features or lower it for fine detail, then generate again.
shared.see: A flat, top-down material image that repeats without a visible edge.
shared.gotcha: Scenario's pricing page says free-plan output is for personal and evaluation use only; paid plans include a commercial licence.

do: In Scenario's 3D viewer, set Geometry to Plane and raise the Tiling slider.
Or in Blender, open the image in the Image Editor and turn on Repeat Image in the sidebar's Display panel.
On a Blender Image Texture node, keep Extension set to Repeat.
shared.see: No seams, and no obvious repeating blotches across several tiles.

shared.h: Turn the image into material maps
do: In Scenario's 3D viewer, click Generate Maps to get height, normal, metallic, edge and AO maps.
Adjust the Raised, Shiny, Polished and Angular sliders, and invert the height map if the relief looks backwards.
For a roughness map, run Scenario's Texture Converter on the colour texture; it outputs normal, roughness, height and metallic maps.
shared.see: A matching set of greyscale maps plus a purple-blue normal map.
shared.gotcha: Generate Maps doesn't produce a roughness map; use the Texture Converter for that.

shared.h: Hook up and check the maps in Blender
do: Add an Image Texture node for each map and connect the colour texture to Base Color on the Principled BSDF.
Set the normal, roughness, AO and height images to Color Space: Non-Color.
Send the normal map through a Normal Map node (Tangent space) into the BSDF's Normal input.
If the bumps look inverted, switch the Normal Map node's convention (Blender uses OpenGL by default).
shared.see: Light catches the relief correctly as you orbit the view.
shared.gotcha: Normal maps must not get colour conversion, so always set them to Non-Color.

do: Open the normal texture and set Compression Settings to Normalmap; tick Flip Green Channel if the bumps look inverted.
Open the roughness and AO textures and untick sRGB, because data maps shouldn't be gamma-corrected.
steps.see: Normal shading looks right and the roughness keeps its values.
steps.gotcha: After turning sRGB off, set that texture's sampler to Linear Color in the material, or it won't compile.

do: Right-click in the Content Browser, choose Material, and double-click it to open.
Add one Texture Sample node per map.
Connect colour to Base Color, roughness to Roughness, normal to Normal and AO to Ambient Occlusion.
steps.see: The preview sphere shows the finished material.
steps.gotcha: The Ambient Occlusion input only has an effect with Static or Stationary lights.

do: Select the normal map and set Texture Type to Normal map; use Flip Green Channel for DirectX-style maps.
On data textures (metallic/smoothness, AO, mask maps), turn off sRGB (Color Texture).
steps.see: The normal map imports as a Normal map texture and shades correctly.

do: Create a material with the Lit shader and set Workflow Mode to Metallic.
Assign the Base Map, Normal Map, Height Map and Occlusion Map.
Unity uses smoothness, not roughness: invert the roughness map, put it in the Metallic Map's alpha, and set Smoothness Source to Metallic Alpha.
steps.see: Reflections are sharp where the roughness map was dark.
steps.gotcha: HDRP uses a packed Mask Map instead: red = metallic, green = AO, blue = detail mask, alpha = smoothness.

do: Select the normal map, and in the Import dock set Compress > Normal Map to Enable.
For DirectX-style maps, also enable Process > Normal Map Invert Y, then click Reimport.
steps.see: The texture reimports as a normal map.

do: Add a StandardMaterial3D to the mesh and set Albedo > Texture.
Set Roughness > Texture (it reads the red channel by default).
Enable Normal Map and Ambient Occlusion and assign those textures; height is optional.
Raise UV1 > Scale to repeat the tile across the surface.
steps.see: The surface tiles and reacts properly to light.
steps.gotcha: Height is a parallax effect and is fairly expensive on the GPU, so use it only where it shows.
